activities.anchor: Knowing that evaluation order explains the classic beginner errors
activities.caption: sequence the logical evaluation pipeline
activities.name: sqlLogicalOrder

config.prompt: The engine rewrites your lines into this order — put the pipeline in sequence:
items: GROUP BY — which rows collapse together
SELECT — which columns and computed expressions appear
config.why: Every analysis, however long, is this pipeline repeated and layered — and each beginner error is a step run where it does not exist yet.

activities.anchor: The engine reorders your query into its logical pipeline
activities.caption: find the faulty line — clauses out of place
activities.name: sqlWrittenSpot

config.prompt: One of these claims about clause placement is backwards — click it:
lines: WHERE filters rows before groups exist.
HAVING filters groups after they are formed.
A row condition placed in HAVING is the clearest way to filter rows.
ORDER BY and LIMIT run last, at presentation.
config.correction: Row conditions belong in WHERE — a row condition in HAVING works only by accident, and the placement tells the reader where your condition acts.
config.why: A group condition in WHERE fails outright; a row condition in HAVING quietly misleads whoever reads the query next.

activities.caption: fill the blanks — the mechanical defences
activities.name: sqlGrainCloze

config.text: The mechanical defences against silent grain changes: state the %%0%% in a comment at the top of each CTE; check row counts with %%1%% — the analyst's pulse; and aggregate the many side %%2%% joining, so the fan-out never happens.
config.hint: The habit of habits, the pulse, and the timing that starves the fan-out.

activities.anchor: which is exactly the population churn analysis needs
activities.caption: pair each join with its population
activities.name: sqlJoinMatch

config.prompt: Join type is a population decision — pair each with who survives:

pairs.right: only rows matching on both sides — orphans silently excluded
every left row kept; the right side filled with NULLs
everything from both sides, matched where possible

config.why: The join you choose silently defines who is in the analysis at all — which is why the choice deserves a comment, not a reflex.

activities.anchor: One refinement that separates careful analysts
activities.caption: WHERE or HAVING? file each condition
activities.name: sqlWhereSort

config.prompt: Rows before grouping, groups after — file each condition:

items.label: months with revenue above the target
segments averaging at least two orders

config.why: Every column in SELECT must be in the GROUP BY or inside an aggregate — the database refuses anything else, forcing you to declare what one output row means.

activities.caption: true or false — NULL's house rules
activities.name: sqlNullJudge

statements.why: It evaluates to NULL — unknown — so equality filters silently exclude nulls.

statements.s: NOT IN with a NULL in the list can return nothing at all.
statements.why: The famous trap — the unknown comparison poisons every row.

statements.s: COALESCE(a, b) substitutes b whenever a is missing.
statements.why: Used thoughtfully: 'no sale' and 'sale of 0' are different facts a blanket COALESCE erases.

statements.s: IS NULL is the correct test for missingness.
statements.why: Never = NULL — the equals test cannot see it.

activities.anchor: The two canonical analysts' questions are now one-liners
activities.caption: GROUP BY vs window functions — drag the divider
activities.name: sqlWindowCompare

config.prompt: The aggregation lens versus the window — drag between them:

before.label: GROUP BY
before.text: Collapses rows into one row per group: revenue per month arrives, and the individual rows are destroyed on the way.

after.label: Window functions
after.text: Compute across rows while keeping them: each row carries its partition's rank, running total or average alongside its own value — LAG even puts last month on this month's row.

config.why: A window's PARTITION BY is a shadow GROUP BY — its grain still needs stating, or the plausible-looking table grows again.

activities.caption: audit a teammate's query — walk the review
activities.name: sqlCteBranch

config.root: A teammate hands you a 200-line query of nested subqueries. Walk the review.

choices.label: Rewrite as a CTE chain — one named step per stage, grain in a comment
choices.feedback: Each CTE can be run, counted and eyeballed independently — debugging becomes isolating one stage.

choices.label: Run it top to bottom and trust the output
choices.feedback: Wrong SQL rarely errors — a bad join returns a big, plausible-looking table; trust is not a review.

check.text: One CTE returns double the expected rows.

choices.label: Compare row counts to the upstream CTE and hunt the step that doubled the rows
choices.feedback: Row growth after a join is a question to ask, not a success to enjoy — the pulse never lies twice.

choices.label: Silence it with a LIMIT and move on
choices.feedback: A LIMIT hides the symptom, not the cause — the duplicates still flow into every aggregate downstream.

done.text: Grain stated, counts checked, one purpose per step: the query now reads as a story a teammate can audit and extend.

trust.text: The deliverable is an analysis someone can re-run — an unauditable cathedral is an anecdote waiting to be quoted.

limit.text: The doubles survive every sum and average after that LIMIT — and SELECT * up top will break silently the day the schema moves.

config.why: Analysis SQL is read by humans and machines — structure it like code, because it is code.
